kunyah: Abu Abdullah — the confidant of the Prophet ﷺ
tribe: Banu Abs of Ghatafan — allies of the Banu Abd al-Ashhal of al-Aws in Madina
teaser: He watched Muslims kill his own father by mistake, and said, 'May Allah forgive you.'

layers.title: Who
layers.subtitle: An outsider family living under Aws protection
layers.content:
Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman. His father's name was Husayl ibn Jabir, and al-Yaman was what people called him. They were of 'Abs, one of the clans of Ghatafan, living in Madina as allies of the Banu 'Abd al-Ashhal of al-Aws — which is to say they were resident but not native, protected but not of the blood.

His sister was Layla bint al-Yaman, and she had married into the family that sheltered them. Her son, Hudhayfah's nephew, was Salama ibn Thabit.

He was not at Badr. Ibn Sa'd records 'Abdullah ibn Ja'far's careful phrasing about that: even though Hudhayfah was not present at Badr, he became Muslim early on. Somebody thought it necessary to say so, which tells you the absence was noticed and had to be explained.

He was the sort of man other people quoted. Look at how he speaks in the reports and you find the same habit every time: exact, measured, and unwilling to say a syllable more than he had actually seen.
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley — the notice on 'Ammar ibn Yasir for 'Abdullah ibn Ja'far's remark, and entry 94, Salama ibn Thabit, for Layla bint al-Yaman and the alliance with the Banu al-Ashhal

layers.title: The Conversion
layers.subtitle: He missed Badr because he kept his word
layers.content:
Here is why he was not at Badr, in his own account.

He set out with his father to join the Prophet ﷺ, and on the road Quraysh intercepted them. The Makkans asked where they were going, and made them swear they would return to Madina and not fight alongside Muhammad ﷺ. The two of them gave that undertaking, arrived, and put the matter to the Prophet ﷺ. He told them to go back: we will keep our covenant with them, and seek Allah's help against them.

So the greatest day of the early Muslim community happened without him, and it happened without him because a promise extracted by an enemy under duress was still a promise.

That is the first thing on his record. Not a feat. A restraint. He held a piece of his word for people who had no claim on it, and lost Badr for it.

Read the rest of his life with that in view. The man the Prophet ﷺ later trusted with the names of the hypocrites was first tested on whether he could be trusted at all, at the highest cost available to him.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih Muslim, Book of Jihad, narrated by Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman — the covenant with Quraysh and the Prophet's ﷺ instruction to keep it
layers.source: Sahih Muslim, Book of Jihad; Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, for 'Abdullah ibn Ja'far's note that he became Muslim early despite his absence from Badr

layers.title: With the Prophet ﷺ
layers.subtitle: Sent alone into the enemy camp in the cold
layers.content:
On the coldest night of the siege of Madina, with the Confederates encamped outside and the wind tearing their tents apart, the Prophet ﷺ sent one man out to find out what the enemy was doing. Hudhayfah went.

He was given an instruction with it: bring me news of them, and do nothing until you come back to me. He walked into their camp, moved among them, found them breaking up to leave — and came back without acting, though the opportunity was in front of him. He had been told not to.

Then Tabuk, at the end. Coming home, on a mountain pass, twelve hypocrites moved to kill the Prophet ﷺ. There were exactly two men with him: 'Ammar ibn Yasir holding the she-camel's reins, and Hudhayfah driving it. Everyone else had gone down into the valley. Hudhayfah was sent back to see, struck at the faces of their mounts with the crook in his hand, and they scattered.

Afterwards the Prophet ﷺ told him their names and what they had intended. Of that plot Allah says: «وَهَمُّوا بِمَا لَمْ يَنَالُوا» — 'and they resolved upon what they could not attain' (9:74).

That is why he was called the confidant. He was given the list, and he kept it.
layers.quran_ref: Quran 9:74 — applied to the Tabuk plot by al-Mubarakpuri
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih Muslim, Book of Jihad, narrated by Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman — the night reconnaissance at the Trench
layers.source: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the dispatch on the cold night of the Trench and the assassination attempt on the return from Tabuk, with Qur'an 9:74 applied to it; the reconnaissance also in Sahih Muslim, Book of Jihad

layers.title: The Trial and Quality
layers.subtitle: 'Servants of Allah, that is my father'
layers.content:
At Uhud the idolaters broke and ran, and then the dust and the confusion did what no enemy managed. 'A'isha's account, in al-Bukhari, has Iblis calling out from behind the Muslim lines to make them turn on each other. Men who could not tell one another apart began to fight.

And Hudhayfah saw his own father, al-Yaman, surrounded by Muslims about to kill him.

He shouted. 'Servants of Allah, beware, that is my father. That is my father.' They did not hear him. They did not stop until the old man was dead.

What he said next was five words: 'May Allah forgive you.' No blood money was taken. He directed that the compensation owed for his father be given away as charity instead. 'Urwa, narrating from 'A'isha, adds a line about the aftermath: from that day on, Hudhayfah did not stop being provided for until he died.

His family paid twice over that afternoon. His nephew Salama ibn Thabit was killed at Uhud too, by Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, and Salama's father and uncle were killed beside him.

He had every right the law gives a grieving son, and he waived all of it inside a minute. May Allah be pleased with him.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by 'A'isha, transmitted by 'Urwa — the killing of al-Yaman at Uhud and Hudhayfah's words
layers.source: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar, citing the account in Sahih al-Bukhari from 'A'isha; Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, entry 94, for the death of Salama ibn Thabit, his father and his uncle at Uhud

layers.title: The Legacy
layers.subtitle: He knew what was coming and it did not comfort him
layers.content:
Under 'Umar he did ordinary administrative work, and did it honestly. Surveying the tax of Iraq, standing with the caliph, he reported: I have imposed on the land what it can bear, and there is not much excess in it. No inflation of his own performance, no promise of more.

The famous conversation happened at 'Arafat. Their camels stood side by side, knees touching, watching the sun go down over a crowd making takbir. 'Umar liked what he saw and asked how long he thought this would last for people. Hudhayfah said there was a door to trial, and when the door was broken open, it would come out. 'Umar, alarmed, asked what the door was. 'A man will die or be killed.' Then 'Umar asked who he thought the people would put in command after him, and Hudhayfah named 'Uthman.

He was right about all of it, and being right was no consolation. When 'Umar was killed he said the Muslims had left the enclosure of Islam that day, and that Islam under 'Umar had been like a man walking forward and only growing nearer, and after him like a man walking backwards and only growing further away.

When 'Uthman was killed he made a circle with his hand and said an opening had been made in Islam that a mountain could not pass through. He swore: if that killing was good, 'Uthman has no part in it; if it was evil, I am innocent of it.

Reports place his own death in 36 AH, not long after. He is the Companion who was told what was coming, and who spent his last years grieving over it rather than trading on it.
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley — the land survey narrated from 'Amr ibn Maymun, the 'Arafat conversation narrated from Rib'iyy ibn Hirash, the sayings on 'Umar's death narrated from Zahdam al-Jarmi and Rib'iyy ibn Hirash, and the words on 'Uthman's killing narrated from Maymun ibn Mahran and from Ibn Sirin

quiz.prompt: Why was Hudhayfah absent from the Battle of Badr?

options.text: He was too young to fight
Quraysh had intercepted him and made him promise not to fight, and the Prophet ﷺ told him to keep the promise
He was on an errand in Yemen
He had not yet accepted Islam

quiz.citation: Sahih Muslim, Book of Jihad, narrated by Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman
quiz.scholar_reflection: The Prophet ﷺ told him and his father to go back: we keep our covenant with them and seek Allah's help against them. The oath had been extracted under pressure and it still stood.

quiz.prompt: What instruction did the Prophet ﷺ give Hudhayfah when sending him into the Confederates' camp on the cold night of the Trench?

options.text: To set fire to their tents
To bring back one prisoner
To bring news of them and do nothing until he returned
To carry a message to Abu Sufyan

quiz.citation: Sahih Muslim, Book of Jihad, narrated by Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman; al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar
quiz.scholar_reflection: He found the enemy already breaking camp, and came back without doing anything, though he was standing among them in the dark. The instruction was the harder half of the mission.

quiz.prompt: Who was with the Prophet ﷺ when twelve hypocrites attempted to kill him on the return from Tabuk?

options.text: Abu Bakr and 'Umar
Only 'Ammar ibn Yasir and Hudhayfah
A guard of thirty men
Zayd ibn Thabit alone

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — with Qur'an 9:74 applied to the incident
quiz.scholar_reflection: 'Ammar held the reins and Hudhayfah drove the camel. Everyone else had already descended into the valley. Afterwards the Prophet ﷺ told Hudhayfah the plotters' names, and that is where his title comes from.

quiz.prompt: What did Hudhayfah say and do after Muslims killed his father by mistake at Uhud?

options.text: He demanded blood money and it was paid
He named the men responsible to the Prophet ﷺ
He said 'May Allah forgive you' and had the compensation given away as charity
He left Madina for a year in grief

quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by 'A'isha through 'Urwa; cited in al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar
quiz.scholar_reflection: He had shouted 'that is my father, that is my father' and they had not heard him. 'Urwa notes that from that day Hudhayfah did not cease to be provided for until he died.

quiz.prompt: At 'Arafat, 'Umar asked how long the state of the people would last. What did Hudhayfah answer?

options.text: That it would last until the end of time
That there was a door to trial, and it would open when a man died or was killed
That he had not been given knowledge of it
That only the caliph could decide it

quiz.citation: Narrated from Rib'iyy ibn Hirash — Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: 'Umar was alarmed and pressed him on what the door was. He was talking about 'Umar's own murder, standing beside him, knee to knee. And then 'Umar asked who would follow him, and Hudhayfah named 'Uthman.

quiz.prompt: He lost Badr because he honoured a promise forced out of him by the enemy. How binding is a commitment you were pressured into?

options.text: Binding, and I have paid for that view
Not binding — consent under pressure is not consent
It depends who I gave it to
I would keep it and resent it the whole time

quiz.citation: Reflection on Sahih Muslim, Book of Jihad, narrated by Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman
quiz.scholar_reflection: There was a ruling available that would have freed him, and the Prophet ﷺ did not reach for it. He said: we keep our covenant with them, and we seek Allah's help against them.

quiz.prompt: Standing inside the enemy camp with an opportunity in front of him, he did nothing, because he had been told to do nothing. Where is that hardest for you?

options.text: When I can see a better way than the one I was given
When nobody would ever find out
When waiting looks like cowardice to people watching
I find the instruction a relief; I would rather not decide

quiz.citation: Reflection on Sahih Muslim, Book of Jihad, narrated by Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman
quiz.scholar_reflection: He was a scout, alone, unobserved, among men who had come to destroy his city. Restraint in that position is not passivity. It is the harder act.

quiz.prompt: He was given the names of the hypocrites and never used them as leverage. What do you do with information about people that you could use?

options.text: I keep it, but I let people know I have it
I tell one trusted person, which defeats the purpose
I keep it completely, and it weighs on me
I have used something once and I am not proud of it

quiz.citation: Reflection on al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar
quiz.scholar_reflection: He lived for decades in a small society with those men. He knew their faces in the mosque and at funerals, and the list did not come out of him.

quiz.prompt: He forgave his father's killers immediately, before anyone asked him to. What is your honest relationship with forgiving quickly?

options.text: I forgive fast and find the feeling comes back later
I need an apology first, and usually never get one
I have forgiven the large things and not the small ones
There is one thing I am still holding and I know it

quiz.citation: Reflection on Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by 'A'isha through 'Urwa
quiz.scholar_reflection: It was not a hard case. The men were identifiable, the killing was witnessed, and the compensation was owed to him under the law. He waived it and had it given away.

quiz.prompt: He foresaw the trials and it brought him no comfort — he grieved instead. What happens in you when you can see something bad coming?

options.text: I warn people and they do not listen, and I stop warning
I get a bitter satisfaction from being right
I try to prevent it long past the point where I can
I grieve early and am worn out by the time it arrives

quiz.citation: Reflection on Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: He described Islam after 'Umar as a man walking backwards, only ever getting further away. That is not the language of someone enjoying his own accuracy.
